title: AI is eroding office hours, study groups, and the trust between faculty and students, MIT report finds
source_used: The Decoder (fulltext/C14-10.txt, 5,899 chars, HTTP 200); date checked in The Tech, 17 Sep 2026 (dl14/c10_tech.txt)
key_facts: An MIT expert committee wants universities to rethink how they deal with AI; its report documents fewer students at office hours, lower online discussion participation and thinner study groups, and says faculty find it harder to judge what students learn.

The Decoder says the report was published in June 2026; MIT's student newspaper The Tech says the Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning, and Research Training released its final report on 13 Aug 2026 after nine months.

Faculty say policing unauthorised AI use damages their relationships with students; the committee advises against AI-text detectors, which it calls unreliable (they often flag non-native speakers and neurodivergent students) and which risk an arms race with 'AI humanizers'.
Theses and dissertations should disclose AI use and never list AI as a co-author; the committee also recommends transparency rules for faculty use of AI.
It recommends oral exams, semester portfolios, in-person discussion and project-based work, and an AI policy for each course set out in the syllabus, rather than one institute-wide rule.

Faculty considering AI agents instead of students as research assistants would hit the Undergraduate Research Opportunities Program (UROP): 93% of the class of 2025 took part and 58% of faculty served as mentors.

MIT gives all members AI models through its Parley platform (faculty and graduate students get $30 a month in credits) but premium subscriptions cost several hundred dollars a month, and the committee warns that unequal access could drive performance differences.

The Decoder adds outside studies: a Chinese study of more than 26,000 students found AI raised homework grades 18% but exam scores fell 20% after six months; UC Berkeley found the share of A grades in writing- and coding-heavy courses up 13 points since ChatGPT launched; a Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam trial found students using AI did better than the no-AI group.
quote_evidence: The report recommends a shift toward oral exams, semester portfolios, in-person discussions, and project-based work.
AI text detection software is unreliable and often flags work by non-native speakers or neurodivergent students as AI-generated, so the committee explicitly advises against using it.
On Aug. 13, 2026, MIT’s Ad Hoc Committee on AI Use in Teaching, Learning, and Research Training released their final report after nine months of deliberation.
why_it_matters_hint: A leading technical university's committee says AI is changing how students and teachers work together and asks for course-by-course AI rules and assessment changes.
event_date: MIT committee final report released 13 Aug 2026 (The Tech); The Decoder article 5 Oct 2026.
notes: Old news re-dated.
